probes.support_reason: Deterministic tie-break answered YES for every numbered sub-requirement. F-1: (1) `enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } }` declares a type with EXACTLY two alternatives carrying differently shaped, NAMED payloads, and the set is closed by the language's own rules: Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Enumerations' makes an enum's variant list part of its declaration, so a third alternative requires editing this declaration; nothing elsewhere can add one, and the `#[non_exhaustive]` attribute -- which only ever RESTRICTS downstream crates -- is not written. (2) `let s: Shape = Shape::Circle { r: 2.0 };` constructs a `Circle` with r = 2.0 and binds it to a local whose static type is `Shape`, not `Circle`: in Rust a variant is not a type, so `Shape` is the only type the value can have (Reference 'Enumerations'). The R9 substitution clause does NOT apply -- Rust expresses a closed alternative set natively -- so this is FULL, not PARTIAL/P-a. F-2/F-4: core language only. F-3: builds under the frozen recipe and prints 2. F-6: no normative prohibition. R10 record (frozen tokenizer): selected named-field form = 35 tokens; the tuple-variant form `enum Shape { Circle(f64), Rect(f64, f64) } let s: Shape = Shape::Circle(2.0);` = 27 tokens and is excluded BEFORE R10, by R1: sub-requirement (1) names the fields `r`, `w` and `h`, and tuple variants drop those names. The annotation `let s: Shape` is kept rather than the inferable `let s` (33 tokens) because sub-requirement (2) states that `s`'s static type is `Shape`. AUDIT CORRECTION (F14.P1 fact ledger): the three field sites `r`, `w` and `h` previously carried NO rows of their own; their content was folded into the type-declaration rows. Methodology 02 section 1.1 makes S1 explicitly include 'field' and section 3.1 caps at one row per (site, kind), not one row per group of sites; A3.4 ('Different entities -> not duplicates') forbids collapsing three fields into one row. Only quidra and python had enumerated field sites, which was the single largest driver of the density spread on this probe. Zig's 'counted once ... anti-double-counted' note misapplies A3.3, which makes a later row DUP only when the fact concerns the same entity or the same operation. [CROSS-LANGUAGE CONSISTENCY AUDIT 2026-09-18]

probes.support_reason: Deterministic tie-break answered YES for every numbered sub-requirement. F-1: (1) `match s { ... }` dispatches over `s`'s alternatives with one arm per variant and NO `_`, no `..` and no catch-all arm; Rust's match is required to be exhaustive and rustc rejects a non-exhaustive one (E0004), so the construct itself carries the check. (2) the area is computed per alternative -- 3.141592653589793 * r * r for `Circle`, w * h for `Rect` -- and bound to the 64-bit floating-point local `area`; (3) `area` is the fragment's tail expression and therefore its result. F-2/F-4: core language only. F-3: builds under the frozen recipe and prints 12.566370614359172 for the `Circle { r: 2.0 }` of F14.P1. F-6: no normative prohibition. R10 record (frozen tokenizer): selected `match` form = 37 tokens; the equivalent `if let` chain `if let Shape::Circle { r } = s { ... } else if let Shape::Rect { w, h } = s { ... } else { 0.0 }` = 46 tokens and is additionally excluded by sub-requirement (1), because the trailing `else` IS a catch-all arm. R10 and the task agree. OBSERVATION TARGET (scored by B/D only): a reader CAN determine that the language guarantees all alternatives are covered -- Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Match expressions' states that the patterns must be irrefutable as a set -- and CAN determine what happens if one is not: nothing happens at run time, because the program does not build (verified: removing the `Rect` arm yields E0004 'non-exhaustive patterns: `Shape::Rect { .. }` not covered'). AUDIT CORRECTION (F14.P2 fact ledger): the ledger has been completed site by site against the methodology 02 section 1.2 applicability matrix, which fixes the rows and leaves only their DISPOSITION to the language. The pre-audit ledger recorded only the rows the analyst found interesting (14 counted), and in particular the `Shape::Rect { w, h }` binder site carried ZERO rows while `Shape::Circle { r }` carried three, although E7 makes each declarator its own site. Rows that the external `Shape` declaration is needed to settle are recorded as LOOKUP rather than omitted, per section 1.3 ('a silent NA is forbidden'). [CROSS-LANGUAGE CONSISTENCY AUDIT 2026-09-18] AUDIT CONFIRMATION (F14.P2 support): re-checked and unchanged at FULL, 2.0/2 -- the R10 construct for a closed alternative set, no default/else/catch-all arm written, area computed per alternative into a 64-bit float local, area produced, and a verified build-and-run. The exhaustiveness question is an OBSERVATION TARGET scored by metrics B/D only, not a support requirement. [CROSS-LANGUAGE CONSISTENCY AUDIT 2026-09-18]

determinacy_enumeration: V1 -- `Shape` IS A `Copy` ENUM WITH `f64` FIELDS. Axis vector: A1 = copy (the scrutinee is duplicated; `s` remains usable after the fragment); A4 = binary floating point; A6 = cannot fail (built-in IEEE-754 multiplication is total, producing Inf rather than trapping, and Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Overflow' does not apply to floating point); A7 = target fixed by compile-time information; A9 = falls through. Witness p14p2v1.rs, frozen recipe entry `rust`, observer output '6 6' -- the caller reads `s` a second time, which only the copy interpretation permits.

V2 -- `Shape` IS A NON-`Copy` ENUM WITH `f64` FIELDS. A1 = move/consume: the match moves the scrutinee and `s` is invalidated for the caller, which is observable outside the fragment (dimension 1). Rule 1.4.4 collapses the whole A1 = move subtree to a single outcome. Witness p14p2v2.rs, observer output 12.566370614359172; the second read of `s` that V1's observer performs is rejected by rustc here (E0382), which is the distinguishing observation.

V3 -- `Shape`'s FIELDS ARE USER TYPES WITH USER `Mul` IMPLEMENTATIONS (Rule 1.4.6 family collapse, merged under Rule 1.4.5). Rule 1.4.7 counts this because a user-redefinable operator makes classes reachable that the built-in cannot: A6 = may trap/panic/abort, A9 = may unwind, and allocation and mutation become reachable inside the arms. Witness p14p2v3.rs: `struct M(f64)` with `impl Mul<M> for f64` and `impl Mul<M> for M`; the fragment is byte-identical and the run panics with 'user Mul: 2 3', exit 101, where V1/V2 return a number.

hidden_items.why: At the arm bodies `3.141592653589793 * r * r` and `w * h` the concrete body is the built-in floating-point multiplication only if the field types are primitives; otherwise Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Arithmetic and Logical Binary Operators' makes `a * b` a `std::ops::Mul::mul` call, and `Mul` is user-implementable. Witness p14p2v3.rs is a candidate that panics where the built-in returns, so the per-candidate equivalence exclusion cannot be recorded and the LED test fails.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 -- Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: `match s` either COPIES the scrutinee or MOVES it, and nothing at the local site says which: the choice is made by whether `Shape` implements `Copy`, declared elsewhere. The difference is material -- in the move case `s` is invalidated for every later use, which witnesses p14p2v1.rs and p14p2v2.rs distinguish (the first reads `s` again and builds; the second is rejected with E0382). Rust marks a borrow with `&` and a clone with `.clone()`, but marks a move with nothing at all, so this is precisely an implicit ownership transfer with no local token.

hidden_items.why: At `let s: &dyn shapes::Shape = &Tri { b: 3.0, h: 4.0 };` the lifetime of the borrowed temporary is silently EXTENDED from the end of the statement to the end of the enclosing block. Nothing at the site says so: the identical expression written as `let s = f(&Tri { ... });` would drop the temporary at the semicolon. The rule is syntactic and depends on the shape of the initializer, which Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Destructors > Temporary lifetime extension' states as a list of extending expression forms, and the difference is material -- without extension the program does not compile, and with a `Drop`-implementing payload it would change when the destructor runs. No local token names the extension, so the LED test fails. NOTE the direction: the DISPATCH at `s.area()` does NOT trigger H3 here, because `dyn` is written at the site and the reference defines it as vtable dispatch, and the unsized coercion does NOT trigger H7, because the target type is written at the same binding.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 -- Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: `if x > y { x } else { y }` moves the chosen operand out as the result and leaves the other to be DESTROYED at the end of the function body, running `T`'s destructor. determinacy_enumeration: V1 -- THE STANDARD `Vec` AND `vec!`. The trait, both concrete types, both impls, the sequence and the call are all inside the fragment; the only external names are `Vec` and `vec!`. Axis vector: A1 = alias to the operand's own storage for the elements (`&A`, `&B`, constant-promoted to `'static`); A4 = text for the produced value and pointer/handle for the elements; A6 = cannot fail (index 0 on a two-element literal sequence; both bodies return literals); A7 = the target may differ between executions of this span (vtable dispatch), which under Rule 1.4.7 adds NO branch because every execution lands in one of the two total bodies written here; A8 = allocation occurs at the named `vec!` and the buffer is deallocated at the end of the block; A9 = falls through. Witness: the frozen probe file, frozen recipe entry `rust`, observer output a.

V2 -- A PRELUDE NAME SHADOWED FROM OUTSIDE THE FRAGMENT. `Vec` and `vec!` are standard-prelude names written in this fragment, and Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Preludes' states that prelude names can be shadowed by explicitly declared items, a macro name by a `macro_rules!` definition earlier in the crate. The family (Rule 1.4.6 collapse, merged under Rule 1.4.5) realizes arbitrary user code at those positions: A6 = may trap/panic/abort, A7 = the name is user-redefinable, A8 = an arbitrary resource event, arbitrary observable result. Witness p15p3v2.rs: a user `macro_rules! vec` that swaps the two elements, declared OUTSIDE the fragment, with the fragment byte-identical; the program builds under the frozen recipe and prints "b" instead of "a".

hidden_items.why: `Vec` and `vec!` are written at the local site with no path qualifying them, and Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Preludes' states that the prelude's names hold only until an explicitly declared item shadows them. Candidate cardinality >= 2, and witness p15p3v2.rs is a shadowing candidate whose observable result differs ("b" instead of "a"), so the per-candidate equivalence exclusion cannot be recorded.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 -- Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: At the distinct local site `items[0].tag()` the concrete body is selected at run time from the element's vtable, and the site's declared element type `&dyn Named` deliberately does not name it. The candidate set is both impls written in the fragment, cardinality 2, and they differ observably ("a" versus "b"), so the equivalence exclusion cannot be recorded. The `dyn` token signals that the dispatch is dynamic, but it does not fix which body runs, which is what H3 tests. This is the probe's own subject matter and a legitimate charge rather than an artefact -- the same event would be charged against any language for the same construct.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 -- Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: The `Vec` bound to `items` is DESTROYED at the end of the enclosing block -- running `Vec`'s `Drop` implementation and returning its heap buffer to the allocator -- with no token written for it. The checklist's own LED illustration puts this case on the triggering side. Note the direction: the ALLOCATION does not trigger, because `vec![...]` is exactly the 'container literal / allocating macro' the checklist excludes.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 -- Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: A distinct rule at a distinct site: `&A` and `&B` are silently CONSTANT-PROMOTED from frame temporaries to values in static memory (Rust Reference (rustc 1.95.0, Edition 2024), https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/ 'Destructors > Constant promotion'), which changes where the data lives and how long it lives, with nothing written at the site. The effect is material and observable to a conforming program: the fragment's result can be returned as `&'static str` from the enclosing function, which a frame temporary could not support (E0515). The promotion rule is also conditional -- it applies only because `A` and `B` have no interior mutability, no `Drop` and no failing initializer -- so a small change to the types silently withdraws it.
